Dear Dr. Vance,

Thank you for evaluating Lucas Miller, an 11-year-old boy whom I have been following in our clinic. His parents first noted ocular changes and mild visual tracking difficulties when he was four years of age.

On our latest assessment, his best-corrected visual acuity was limited to 20/60 in the right eye and 20/50 in the left. Anterior segment examination reveals bilateral corneal enlargement, with horizontal white-to-white diameters measuring roughly 13.5 mm. Ultrasonic pachymetry indicates markedly reduced central corneal thickness, averaging 410 microns bilaterally. His anterior chambers are remarkably deep, though the iridocorneal angles appear open without peripheral anterior synechiae. Intraocular pressures have been consistently normal on applanation tonometry, recording 14 mmHg in the right eye and 15 mmHg in the left today.

The remainder of his ocular exam is non-contributory. His crystalline lenses are clear without phacodonesis or subluxation. Dilated funduscopic examination reveals healthy optic nerves with small physiological cups, flat retinas, and normal foveal contours. Extraocular motility is intact, and pupils are equally round and reactive to light. Lucas is otherwise healthy, takes no daily medications, and enjoys playing recreational soccer. There is no family history of childhood ocular disorders.

I would be very grateful for your expert anterior segment assessment and recommendations regarding his ongoing care.

Warm regards,

Dr. Arthur Jenkins
